claim: Approximately 40% of ERα-positive breast cancer patients suffer from therapeutic resistance to tamoxifen.
source: Approximately 40% ERα-positive breast cancer patients suffer from therapeutic resistance to tamoxifen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Reduced ERα level is the major cause of tamoxifen resistance.
source: Although reduced ERα level is the major cause of tamoxifen resistance, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing from the scientific consensus in the field.

claim: FRMD8 raises the level of ERα at both transcriptional and post-translational layers.
source: Here, we report that FRMD8 raises the level of ERα at both transcriptional and post-translational layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4, showing FRMD8's effects on ESR1 transcription and ERα protein stability.

claim: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice accelerates mammary tumor growth.
source: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice accelerates mammary tumor growth and loss of luminal phenotype, and confers tamoxifen resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-H, demonstrating increased tumor burden in Frmd8-deficient mice.

claim: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice causes loss of luminal phenotype.
source: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice accelerates mammary tumor growth and loss of luminal phenotype, and confers tamoxifen resistance.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1I, 2F, and 3A-B showing decreased expression of luminal markers.

claim: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice confers tamoxifen resistance.
source: FRMD8 deficiency in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice accelerates mammary tumor growth and loss of luminal phenotype, and confers tamoxifen resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1L-O showing that Frmd8-deficient mice do not respond to tamoxifen treatment.

claim: Single-cell RNA profiling reveals that Frmd8 loss decreases the proportion of hormone-sensing differentiated epithelial cells.
source: Single-cell RNA profiling reveals that Frmd8 loss decreases the proportion of hormone-sensing differentiated epithelial cells and downregulates the levels of ERα.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Frmd8 loss downregulates the levels of ERα.
source: Single-cell RNA profiling reveals that Frmd8 loss decreases the proportion of hormone-sensing differentiated epithelial cells and downregulates the levels of ERα.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data in Figure 2L and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Loss of FRMD8 inhibits ESR1 transcription via suppressing the expression of FOXO3A.
source: Mechanically, on one hand, loss of FRMD8 inhibits ESR1 transcription via suppressing the expression of FOXO3A, a transcription factor of ESR1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F-J showing that FRMD8 depletion decreases FOXO3A levels and ESR1 transcription.

claim: FOXO3A is a transcription factor of ESR1.
source: Mechanically, on one hand, loss of FRMD8 inhibits ESR1 transcription via suppressing the expression of FOXO3A, a transcription factor of ESR1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jia et al., 2019 in the Introduction and by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 3J.

claim: FRMD8 interacts with ERα.
source: On the other hand, FRMD8 interacts both with ERα and UBE3A, and disrupts the interaction of UBE3A with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα degradation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: FRMD8 interacts with UBE3A.
source: On the other hand, FRMD8 interacts both with ERα and UBE3A, and disrupts the interaction of UBE3A with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα degradation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5F-G and mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: FRMD8 disrupts the interaction of UBE3A with ERα.
source: On the other hand, FRMD8 interacts both with ERα and UBE3A, and disrupts the interaction of UBE3A with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα degradation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5H-I showing increased ERα-UBE3A interaction upon FRMD8 depletion.

claim: FRMD8 blocks UBE3A-mediated ERα degradation.
source: On the other hand, FRMD8 interacts both with ERα and UBE3A, and disrupts the interaction of UBE3A with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα degradation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B-D showing increased ERα degradation upon FRMD8 depletion, and Figure 5J-K showing rescue by UBE3A depletion.

claim: FRMD8 gene promoter is hypermethylated in breast cancer patients.
source: In breast cancer patients, FRMD8 gene promoter is found hypermethylated and low level of FRMD8 predicts poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 6C and 5-Aza-dC treatment experiments in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Low level of FRMD8 predicts poor prognosis in breast cancer patients.
source: In breast cancer patients, FRMD8 gene promoter is found hypermethylated and low level of FRMD8 predicts poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by tissue microarray analysis and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6F-J.

claim: FRMD8 is an important regulator of ERα.
source: Therefore, FRMD8 is an important regulator of ERα and may control therapeutic sensitivity to tamoxifen in ERα-positive breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing FRMD8's effects on ERα transcription and protein stability.

claim: FRMD8 may control therapeutic sensitivity to tamoxifen in ERα-positive breast cancer patients.
source: Therefore, FRMD8 is an important regulator of ERα and may control therapeutic sensitivity to tamoxifen in ERα-positive breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the mouse model data showing tamoxifen resistance in Frmd8-deficient mice (Figure 1L-O).

claim: More than 70% of breast cancers are estrogen receptor α (ERα)-positive.
source: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide (Sung et al., 2021), and more than 70% of breast cancer are estrogen receptor α (ERα)-positive (Habara and Shimada, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Habara and Shimada, 2022.

claim: Approximately 40% of ERα-positive breast cancer patients develop primary or secondary resistance to endocrine therapy.
source: Although endocrine therapy is the most common systemic treatment for ERα-positive breast cancer in clinical practice, approximately 40% of patients still develop primary or secondary resistance to endocrine therapy (Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016.

claim: ERα is a ligand-activated transcription factor that is activated by estrogen and promotes cell proliferation during breast cancer development.
source: ERα is a ligand-activated transcription factor that is activated by estrogen and promotes cell proliferation during breast cancer development (Harbeck et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harbeck et al., 2019 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor antagonist.
source: Tamoxifen (TAM), a selective estrogen receptor antagonist, is the most widely used medicine in endocrine therapy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of breast cancer treatment.

claim: Tamoxifen competes with estrogen to bind with ERα and changes the conformation of ERα.
source: Tamoxifen competes with estrogen to bind with ERα and changes the conformation of ERα, thereby preventing the interaction between co-activators and ERα and inhibiting activation of ERα (Katzenellenbogen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Katzenellenbogen et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The level of ERα is strongly correlated with reactivity and resistance of endocrine therapy.
source: Thus, the level of ERα is strongly correlated with reactivity and resistance of endocrine therapy.
evidence: This is inferred from the established mechanism of tamoxifen action and represents knowledge in the field.

claim: Multiple transcription factors, such as AP-2γ, FOXO3, FOXM1, and GATA3, bind to the promoter region of ESR1 and participate in transcriptional regulation of ESR1.
source: Multiple transcription factors, such as AP-2γ, FOXO3, FOXM1, and GATA3, have been reported to bind to the promoter region of ESR1, the gene encoding ERα, and participate in transcriptional regulation of ESR1 (Jia et al., 2019; Kos et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jia et al., 2019; Kos et al., 2001.

claim: Post-translational modifications of ERα, including phosphorylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination, have effects on subcellular localization, transcriptional activity, and stability of ERα.
source: In addition, post-translational modifications of ERα, including phosphorylation, acetylation, and ubiquitination, also have effects on subcellular localization, transcriptional activity, and stability of ERα (Rogatsky et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2009; Zhou and Slingerland, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rogatsky et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2009; Zhou and Slingerland, 2014.

claim: FRMD8 binds with iRhom and enhances the stability of the iRhom/TACE complex on the cell surface.
source: FRMD8, as a member of FERM domain-containing proteins, has been reported to bind with iRhom and enhance the stability of the iRhom/TACE complex on the cell surface, thereby preventing iRhom/TACE degradation mediated by lysosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Künzel et al., 2018; Oikonomidi et al., 2018.

claim: TACE is responsible for cleaving and releasing TNF.
source: TACE is responsible for cleaving and releasing TNF, and the absence of FRMD8 impairs the production of TNF (Künzel et al., 2018; Oikonomidi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Künzel et al., 2018; Oikonomidi et al., 2018.

claim: The absence of FRMD8 impairs the production of TNF.
source: TACE is responsible for cleaving and releasing TNF, and the absence of FRMD8 impairs the production of TNF (Künzel et al., 2018; Oikonomidi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Künzel et al., 2018; Oikonomidi et al., 2018.

claim: FRMD8 expressions in both microenvironment and tumor cells promote lung tumor growth.
source: Additionally, FRMD8 expressions in both microenvironment and tumor cells promote lung tumor growth (Badenes et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Badenes et al., 2023.

claim: FRMD8 inhibits colon cancer growth by preventing cell cycle progression.
source: FRMD8 inhibits colon cancer growth by preventing cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2023.

claim: FRMD8 disrupts the interaction of CDK7 with CDK4, subsequently inhibiting CDK4 activation.
source: FRMD8 disrupts the interaction of CDK7 with CDK4, subsequently inhibiting CDK4 activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2023.

claim: FRMD8 competes with MDM2 to bind RB, thereby attenuating MDM2-mediated RB degradation.
source: Furthermore, FRMD8 competes with MDM2 to bind RB, thereby attenuating MDM2-mediated RB degradation (Yu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2023.

claim: Compared with MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice, Frmd8 depleted mice significantly promote mammary tumor development.
source: Compared with MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice, Frmd8 depleted in mice significantly promotes mammary tumor development (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The total tumor weight was markedly higher in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice than the control mice.
source: The total tumor weight (Figure 1G) and number of tumors (Figure 1H) were markedly higher in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice than the control mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The number of tumors was markedly higher in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice than the control mice.
source: The total tumor weight (Figure 1G) and number of tumors (Figure 1H) were markedly higher in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice than the control mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The luminal epithelium was poorly differentiated in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice tumors compared with the control mice.
source: Histological examination of the breast tumors from PyMT mice using H&E staining revealed that the luminal epithelium was poorly differentiated in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice tumors compared with the control mice (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The percentage of Ki67-positive cells was significantly elevated in mammary tumors of Frmd8-depleted mice.
source: Furthermore, immunohistochemical staining showed that the percentage of Ki67-positive cells was significantly elevated in mammary tumors of Frmd8-depleted mice (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: Frmd8 deficiency in the luminal epithelium accelerates mammary tumor growth in MMTV-PyMT mice and promotes cell proliferation.
source: These findings indicated that Frmd8 deficiency in the luminal epithelium accelerates mammary tumor growth in MMTV-PyMT mice and promotes cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on tumor growth, Ki67 staining, and histology.

claim: Tamoxifen significantly prevents mammary tumor progression in the control mice.
source: The results showed that tamoxifen significantly prevents mammary tumor progression in the control mice (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Mammary tumors of MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice showed no response to tamoxifen treatment.
source: However, mammary tumors of MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice showed no response to tamoxifen treatment (Figure 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: The total tumor weight of MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice was markedly decreased after tamoxifen treatment.
source: Consistently, the total tumor weight (Figure 1N) and number of tumors (Figure 1O) of MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice were markedly decreased after tamoxifen treatment, whereas there was no difference in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: The number of tumors of MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice was markedly decreased after tamoxifen treatment.
source: Consistently, the total tumor weight (Figure 1N) and number of tumors (Figure 1O) of MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice were markedly decreased after tamoxifen treatment, whereas there was no difference in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: There was no difference in tumor weight or number in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice after tamoxifen treatment.
source: Consistently, the total tumor weight (Figure 1N) and number of tumors (Figure 1O) of MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice were markedly decreased after tamoxifen treatment, whereas there was no difference in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 1N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N and O.

claim: Loss of Frmd8 accelerates mammary tumor growth and generates resistance to tamoxifen therapy in Frmd8-depleted mice.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrated that loss of Frmd8 accelerates mammary tumor growth and generates resistance to tamoxifen therapy in Frmd8-depleted mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on tumor growth and tamoxifen treatment.

claim: Cells that passed quality control filter totaled 24,320 in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Cells that passed quality control (QC) filter totaled 24,320, of which 11,606 cells were from MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT, and 12,714 cells were from MMTV -Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from the scRNA-seq experiment described in the methods and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 11,606 cells were from MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Cells that passed quality control (QC) filter totaled 24,320, of which 11,606 cells were from MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT, and 12,714 cells were from MMTV -Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: 12,714 cells were from MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Cells that passed quality control (QC) filter totaled 24,320, of which 11,606 cells were from MMTV-Cre-; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT, and 12,714 cells were from MMTV -Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: A total of 12 clearly separated cell lineages were identified in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Based on the expression of known markers, a total of 12 clearly separated cell lineages were finally identified (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is data from the scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The proportion of the Hsd epithelial cells was significantly decreased in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice compared to control mice.
source: In contrast to control mice, the proportion of the Hsd epithelial cells was significantly decreased in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Hsd epithelial cells specifically expressed Esr1 and Pgr.
source: Given that Hsd epithelial cells that specifically expressed Esr1 and Pgr had lower CNV score than alveolar progenitor (Avp), basal (Bsl), and luminal progenitor (Lp) epithelial cells, we defined the low CNV score Hsd epithelial cells as normal cells (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Hsd epithelial cells had lower CNV score than alveolar progenitor (Avp), basal (Bsl), and luminal progenitor (Lp) epithelial cells.
source: Given that Hsd epithelial cells that specifically expressed Esr1 and Pgr had lower CNV score than alveolar progenitor (Avp), basal (Bsl), and luminal progenitor (Lp) epithelial cells, we defined the low CNV score Hsd epithelial cells as normal cells (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The expression of Frmd8 was decreased in tumor cells compared with normal cells.
source: The results also showed that the expression of Frmd8 was decreased in tumor cells compared with normal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and E.

claim: Loss of Frmd8 significantly decreased the expression of Esr1 and Pgr in normal cells of mammary tumors.
source: In addition, we observed that loss of Frmd8 significantly decreased the expression of Esr1 and Pgr in normal cells of mammary tumors and decreased expression of Frmd8 in tumor cells accompanied with low expression of Esr1 and Pgr compared with normal cells (Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Decreased expression of Frmd8 in tumor cells is accompanied with low expression of Esr1 and Pgr compared with normal cells.
source: In addition, we observed that loss of Frmd8 significantly decreased the expression of Esr1 and Pgr in normal cells of mammary tumors and decreased expression of Frmd8 in tumor cells accompanied with low expression of Esr1 and Pgr compared with normal cells (Figure 2L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Frmd8 depletion leads to decreases of the Hsd epithelial cells proportion and the expression of Esr1 and Pgr.
source: Taken together, these findings indicated that Frmd8 depletion in PyMT mice leads to decreases of the Hsd epithelial cells proportion and the expression of Esr1 and Pgr.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined scRNA-seq data.

claim: Deficiency of Frmd8 dramatically decreased the levels of ERα, PR, and CK8 in normal tissues adjacent to tumors.
source: Consistent with the scRNA-seq results, deficiency of Frmd8 dramatically decreased the levels of ERα, PR, and CK8, a marker of mammary luminal epithelium, in normal tissues adjacent to tumors (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: In normal tissues adjacent to tumor of the control mice, the proportion of ERα-positive cells among CK8+ cells were 45.49%.
source: In situ tissue flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that in normal tissues adjacent to tumor of the control mice, the proportion of ERα-positive cells among CK8+ cells were 45.49%, whereas this proportion was just 9.28% in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ tissue flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In normal tissues adjacent to tumor of MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice, the proportion of ERα-positive cells among CK8+ cells was 9.28%.
source: In situ tissue flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that in normal tissues adjacent to tumor of the control mice, the proportion of ERα-positive cells among CK8+ cells were 45.49%, whereas this proportion was just 9.28% in MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ tissue flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The proportion of PR-positive cells among CK8+ cells was reduced in normal tissues adjacent to tumor of MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice compared with the control mice.
source: Similarly, the proportion of PR-positive cells among CK8+ cells was also reduced in normal tissues adjacent to tumor of MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice compared with the control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ tissue flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In mammary tumor tissues from both control mice and MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice, the expressions of ERα and PR were almost negative.
source: In mammary tumor tissues from both control mice and MMTV-Cre+; Frmd8fl/fl; PyMT mice, the expressions of ERα and PR were almost negative (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by multiplex immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Frmd8 depletion markedly decreased the expression of ERα in normal and atypical hyperplasia breast tissues.
source: The results showed that Frmd8 depletion also markedly decreased the expression of ERα in normal and atypical hyperplasia breast tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The deficiency of FRMD8 downregulates the protein levels of ERα and PR in mammary tissues of MMTV-PyMT mice and accelerates the loss of luminal phenotype in mammary gland.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that the deficiency of FRMD8 downregulates the protein levels of ERα and PR in mammary tissues of MMTV-PyMT mice and accelerates the loss of luminal phenotype in mammary gland.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: FRMD8 overexpression drastically increased the levels of ERα.
source: Our results showed that FRMD8 overexpression drastically increased the levels of ERα, while ERα expression was greatly downregulated when FRMD8 was knocked down (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ERα expression was greatly downregulated when FRMD8 was knocked down.
source: Our results showed that FRMD8 overexpression drastically increased the levels of ERα, while ERα expression was greatly downregulated when FRMD8 was knocked down (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Depletion of FRMD8 significantly decreased the mRNA level of ESR1.
source: Moreover, qRT-PCR results indicated that depletion of FRMD8 significantly decreased the mRNA level of ESR1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: FRMD8 silencing dramatically decreased the level of FOXO3A.
source: The results showed that FRMD8 silencing dramatically decreased the level of FOXO3A (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Overexpression of FRMD8 in MCF7 and T47D cells markedly raised the level of FOXO3A.
source: Consistently, overexpression of FRMD8 in MCF7 and T47D cells markedly raised the level of FOXO3A (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Exogenous FRMD8 significantly upregulated ERα expression, but depletion of endogenous FOXO3A greatly reduced the effect of FRMD8 on ERα.
source: Although exogenous FRMD8 significantly upregulated ERα expression, depletion of endogenous FOXO3A greatly reduced the effect of FRMD8 on ERα (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: Depletion of FRMD8 significantly decreased the occupancy of FOXO3A at the ESR1 promoters.
source: Besides, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR was performed and revealed that depletion of FRMD8 significantly decreased the occupancy of FOXO3A at the ESR1 promoters (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: FRMD8 promoted upregulation of ESR1 is mediated by FOXO3A.
source: Altogether, these data indicated that FRMD8 promoted upregulation of ESR1 is mediated by FOXO3A (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on FRMD8, FOXO3A, and ESR1.

claim: Decreased expression of FRMD8 led to a decreased level of exogenous Flag-ERα.
source: Although our results suggest that FRMD8 depletion inhibits the mRNA level of ESR1, unexpectedly, we also observed that decreased expression of FRMD8 led to a decreased level of exogenous Flag-ERα (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: FRMD8 may regulate ERα protein expression at the post-translational level.
source: This result suggested that in addition to inhibiting mRNA expression of ERα, FRMD8 may also regulate ERα protein expression at the post-translational level.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that exogenous ERα is affected by FRMD8 depletion.

claim: Depletion of FRMD8 greatly increased the ERα turnover rate and the half-life of ERα decreased from 6 h to approximately 2 h.
source: Depletion of FRMD8 greatly increased the ERα turnover rate and the half-life of ERα decreased from 6 h to approximately 2 h (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The reduction of ERα levels by FRMD8 depletion was blocked by treatment with MG132 but not CQ.
source: The results showed that the reduction of ERα levels by FRMD8 depletion was blocked by treatment with MG132 but not CQ (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data with proteasome and lysosome inhibitors shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FRMD8 stabilizes ERα protein by inhibiting its degradation via a proteasome-mediated pathway.
source: Altogether, these data suggested that FRMD8 stabilizes ERα protein by inhibiting its degradation via a proteasome-mediated pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on ERα turnover and inhibitor experiments.

claim: FRMD8 interacts with ERα in MCF7 cells.
source: The results showed that FRMD8 interacts with ERα (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FRMD8 interacts with ERα in T47D cells.
source: The results showed that FRMD8 interacts with ERα (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: An interaction between endogenous FRMD8 and endogenous ERα was observed in MCF7 cells.
source: Importantly, an interaction between endogenous FRMD8 and endogenous ERα was also observed in MCF7 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: FRMD8 interacts directly with ERα in vitro.
source: The results indicated that FRMD8 interacts directly with ERα in vitro (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: FRMD8 is a binding partner of ERα in human cells.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that FRMD8 is a binding partner of ERα in human cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined co-IP and GST pull-down data.

claim: UBE3A is a ubiquitin ligase for ERα.
source: Interestingly, UBE3A, a ubiquitin ligase for ERα (Sun et al., 2012), is the only matched protein that interacts with FRMD8 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: UBE3A is the only matched protein that interacts with FRMD8 among known E3 ubiquitin ligases of ERα.
source: Interestingly, UBE3A, a ubiquitin ligase for ERα (Sun et al., 2012), is the only matched protein that interacts with FRMD8 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry analysis and Venn diagram shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is an interaction between FRMD8 and UBE3A.
source: We thus examined the interaction between FRMD8 and UBE3A through co-IP. The results indicated an interaction between FRMD8 and UBE3A (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The level of ERα ubiquitination was markedly increased by FRMD8 depletion.
source: In both cell types, the level of ERα ubiquitination and the interaction between ERα and UBE3A were markedly increased by FRMD8 depletion (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: The interaction between ERα and UBE3A was markedly increased by FRMD8 depletion.
source: In both cell types, the level of ERα ubiquitination and the interaction between ERα and UBE3A were markedly increased by FRMD8 depletion (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: FRMD8 depletion led to a marked decrease of ERα expression, while depletion of UBE3A dramatically rescued the effect of FRMD8 depletion.
source: Intriguingly, FRMD8 depletion led to a marked decrease of ERα expression, while depletion of UBE3A dramatically rescued the effect of FRMD8 depletion (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5J and K.

claim: FRMD8 binds to ERα and UBE3A, and prevents UBE3A interaction with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα ubiquitination and degradation.
source: Taken together, these results strongly demonstrated that FRMD8 binds to ERα and UBE3A, and prevents UBE3A interaction with ERα, thereby blocking UBE3A-mediated ERα ubiquitination and degradation (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on FRMD8-ERα-UBE3A interactions and ubiquitination.

claim: The level of Frmd8 in normal Hsd epithelial cells was significantly higher than other tumor cells in the mammary tumors from PyMT mice.
source: ScRNA-seq results demonstrated that the level of Frmd8 in normal Hsd epithelial cells was significantly higher than other tumor cells in the mammary tumors from PyMT mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: FRMD8 expression was lower in claudin-low breast cancer cell lines compared with normal mammary epithelial cell line or ERα-positive cell lines.
source: Results showed that FRMD8 expression was lower in claudin-low breast cancer cell lines compared with normal mammary epithelial cell line or ERα-positive cell lines (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The FRMD8 promoter was highly methylated in primary breast tumors.
source: An analysis based on the TCGA database showed that the FRMD8 promoter was highly methylated in primary breast tumors (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by TCGA database analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 5-Aza-dC treatment significantly upregulated both mRNA and protein levels of FRMD8 in claudin-low breast cancer cell lines.
source: The results showed that 5-Aza-dC treatment significantly upregulated both mRNA and protein levels of FRMD8 in claudin-low but not luminal breast cancer cell lines (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with the lower expression of FRMD8 in claudin-low breast cancer cell lines (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: 5-Aza-dC treatment did not significantly upregulate FRMD8 levels in luminal breast cancer cell lines.
source: The results showed that 5-Aza-dC treatment significantly upregulated both mRNA and protein levels of FRMD8 in claudin-low but not luminal breast cancer cell lines (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), which was consistent with the lower expression of FRMD8 in claudin-low breast cancer cell lines (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FRMD8 gene promoter is hypermethylated, which could be the reason for the reduced FRMD8 expression in triple-negative breast cancer cells.
source: These findings demonstrated that FRMD8 gene promoter is hypermethylated, which could be the reason for the reduced FRMD8 expression in triple-negative breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on promoter methylation and 5-Aza-dC treatment effects.

claim: Patients with lower level of FRMD8 showed poor overall survival (p=0.0409).
source: The results suggested that patients with lower level of FRMD8 showed poor overall survival (p=0.0409) (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by tissue microarray analysis and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: A decreased FRMD8 level was associated with poor recurrence-free survival in breast cancer patients.
source: Moreover, we also found that a decreased FRMD8 level was associated with poor recurrence-free survival in breast cancer patients according to Kaplan–Meier Plotter analysis (Figure 6H and J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier Plotter analysis shown in Figure 6H and J.

claim: The promoter of FRMD8 is hypermethylated, and the low FRMD8 level predicts poor prognosis of breast cancer patients.
source: Collectively, these data indicated that the promoter of FRMD8 is hypermethylated, and the low FRMD8 level predicts poor prognosis of breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on promoter methylation and survival analysis.

claim: FRMD8 plays a tumor suppressive role in breast cancer progression.
source: In this study, we found that FRMD8 plays a tumor suppressive role in breast cancer progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data showing that FRMD8 loss promotes tumor growth.

claim: Loss of FRMD8 promotes mammary tumor growth, accelerates the loss of mammary luminal phenotype, and confers tamoxifen resistance via downregulating ERα level.
source: We demonstrated that loss of FRMD8 promotes mammary tumor growth, accelerates the loss of mammary luminal phenotype, and confers tamoxifen resistance via downregulating ERα level.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data throughout the study.

claim: FRMD8 depletion not only suppresses transcription of ESR1 through decreasing the level of FOXO3A, but also promotes the E3 ligase UBE3A binding with ERα to disrupt ERα protein stability.
source: FRMD8 depletion not only suppresses transcription of ESR1 through decreasing the level of FOXO3A, but also promotes the E3 ligase UBE3A binding with ERα to disrupts ERα protein stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on transcriptional and post-translational regulation.

claim: Early-stage mammary tumors in MMTV-PyMT mice express ERα and PR, but these receptors are gradually lost as the tumor progresses.
source: In MMTV-PyMT mice, early-stage mammary tumors express ERα and PR, but these receptors are gradually lost as the tumor progresses (Lapidus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lapidus et al., 1998.

claim: Only Hsd epithelial cells showed ERα and PR expression among mammary tumor epithelial cells in MMTV-PyMT mice.
source: Our scRNA-seq results revealed that mammary tumor epithelial cells in MMTV-PyMT mice fall into four clusters, with only Hsd epithelial cells showing ERα and PR expression.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Hsd epithelial cells exhibited the lowest CNV score, indicating a closer resemblance to normal epithelial cells.
source: Additionally, Hsd epithelial cells exhibited the lowest CNV score, indicating a closer resemblance to normal epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The loss of Frmd8 reduced the proportion of Hsd epithelial cells and led to a downregulation of ERα and PR expression.
source: The loss of Frmd8 reduced the proportion of Hsd epithelial cells and led to a downregulation of ERα and PR expression, implying that Frmd8 deficiency promotes the loss of luminal features in the mammary gland and accelerates mammary tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F and 2L.

claim: Frmd8 deficiency promotes the loss of luminal features in the mammary gland and accelerates mammary tumor progression.
source: The loss of Frmd8 reduced the proportion of Hsd epithelial cells and led to a downregulation of ERα and PR expression, implying that Frmd8 deficiency promotes the loss of luminal features in the mammary gland and accelerates mammary tumor progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined scRNA-seq and tumor growth data.

claim: FOXO3A locates in nucleus and blocks cell cycle progression via activating the cell cycle blocking protein p27KIP1.
source: FOXO3A locates in nucleus and blocks cell cycle progression via activating the cell cycle blocking protein p27KIP1 (Seoane et al., 2004).

claim: FOXO3A contributes to cell death through a Fas ligand-dependent mechanism.
source: In addition, FOXO3A contributes to cell death through a Fas ligand-dependent mechanism (Seoane et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seoane et al., 2004.

claim: Phosphorylated FOXO3A mediated by AKT binds to 14-3-3 protein and remains in the cytoplasm, resulting in loss of activity.
source: Phosphorylated FOXO3A mediated by AKT binds to 14-3-3 protein and remains in the cytoplasm, resulting in loss of activity (Arden, 2004).

claim: FRMD8 may be involved in the regulation of cell cycle or apoptosis in an ERα-independent manner by regulating FOXO3A.
source: Thus, FRMD8 may also be involved in the regulation of cell cycle or apoptosis in an ERα-independent manner by regulating FOXO3A.

claim: FOXO3A is closely associated with the stemness of breast cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, FOXO3A is closely associated with the stemness of breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

source: FOXO3A suppresses breast cancer stem cell properties and tumorigenicity via inhibition of FOXM1/SOX2 signaling (Liu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2017), suggesting that FRMD8 may have an effect on breast cancer stem cells.

claim: FRMD8 may have an effect on breast cancer stem cells.
source: FOXO3A suppresses breast cancer stem cell properties and tumorigenicity via inhibition of FOXM1/SOX2 signaling (Liu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2017), suggesting that FRMD8 may have an effect on breast cancer stem cells.

claim: The proportion of luminal subtype is increasing in new cases of breast cancer.
source: The proportion of luminal subtype is increasing in new cases of breast cancer (Waks and Winer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waks and Winer, 2019.

source: Tamoxifen therapy is one of the most important systemic treatment for ERα+/HER2- subtype breast cancer patients (Waks and Winer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waks and Winer, 2019.

claim: Primary or secondary tamoxifen resistance occurs in about 40% of patients treated with tamoxifen therapy.
source: Unfortunately, primary or secondary tamoxifen resistance occurs in about 40% of patients treated with tamoxifen therapy, and tamoxifen resistance often leads to the development of resistance to other selective estrogen receptor modulators (Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Badia et al., 2007; Légaré and Basik, 2016; Rondón-Lagos et al., 2016.

source: As a regulator of ERα, FRMD8 may be a therapeutic target for rescue tamoxifen resistance.

source: Deficiency of FRMD8 promotes mammary luminal features loss and confers tamoxifen resistance.

source: Our findings indicated that targeting FRMD8 promoter methylation may provide a novel therapeutic approach for reversing tamoxifen resistance.
